title: Average
summary: One guaranteed question in almost every Tier 1 shift: a member joining or leaving, a batsman's innings, or a weighted two-group average. The whole topic collapses to one habit — convert averages to sums (Sum = Avg × n) before touching anything.

subtopics.title: Average & the sum bridge
subtopics.concept:
An average is one number that stands for a whole list: **average = sum ÷ count**. The exam-useful direction is the reverse: **sum = average × count**.

Add k to every value and the average rises by k. Multiply every value by k and the average is multiplied by k.

For lists with equal gaps (consecutive numbers, multiples of k) the average is the **middle term**. Standard lists have fixed averages: first n odd numbers average n, first n even numbers average n + 1.

formulas.name: Definition
formulas.note: The sum form is the one you use.

formulas.name: Shift property
formulas.note: Adding k shifts the average by k; multiplying by k scales it.

tricks.title: Flip to the sum first
tricks.body: Never push averages around. Change them to sums, adjust, divide back at the end.

example.q: The average of 8 numbers is 32.5. Find their sum.

tricks.title: Same operation on every value
tricks.body: Do to the average exactly what is done to each value, in the same order.

example.q: The average of 6 numbers is 15. Each number is multiplied by 3 and then increased by 5. Find the new average.

tricks.title: Equal gaps: jump from the middle
tricks.body: The average of evenly spaced numbers is the middle term. Step out from it instead of adding everything.

example.q: The average of 5 consecutive numbers is 30. Find the largest.

mistakes.wrong: Giving a sum where the question asks for the average.
mistakes.right: Read the last line: total or per-item value? Divide by the count before answering.

mistakes.wrong: Averaging two group averages of different sizes.
mistakes.right: Only totals can be combined. Convert each group to size × average first.

mistakes.wrong: Using the sum formula $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and forgetting to divide by n.
mistakes.right: The formula gives the sum. The average is the sum ÷ n.

mistakes.wrong: Applying just one of two ordered operations (× 3 then + 5).
mistakes.right: Apply both, in the stated order: $15 \times 3 + 5 = 50$.

mistakes.wrong: Stepping by 1 when the list is of consecutive even or odd numbers.
mistakes.right: Consecutive even or odd numbers step by 2. Use the gap of the series.

subtopics.notes:
### What an average is
An average is one number that stands for a whole list. It is what each one gets when the total is shared equally.

Five friends have ₹20, ₹30, ₹25, ₹35 and ₹40. Total = ₹150. Shared equally: $150 \div 5 = ₹30$. So the average is ₹30. Another name for it is the arithmetic mean.

> **Rule:** Average = sum of values ÷ number of values. Turn it around and you get the working tool: sum = average × count.

### The sum bridge
Most exam questions live on the turned-around form **sum = average × count**.

1. Change every average into a sum.
2. Add or subtract with the sums.
3. Divide again only at the last step.

> **Example:** The average of 4 numbers is 25, and three of them are 20, 30 and 18. Sum = $4 \times 25 = 100$. The known values add to 68. Fourth number = $100 - 68 = 32$.

### Properties that save time
- The average always sits between the smallest and the largest value.
- Add k to every value → the average rises by k. Subtract k → it falls by k.
- Multiply every value by k → the average gets multiplied by k. Divide → it gets divided by k.
- Apply changes in the order given: "× 3, then + 5" on an average of 15 gives $15 \times 3 + 5 = 50$.
- Each value's gap from the average (its deviation) adds up to zero across the whole list.

### Standard series averages
Learn this table by heart. Here n is the **count of terms**, not the last term.

| Series | Average |
|---|---|
| First n natural numbers | $\dfrac{n+1}{2}$ |
| First n odd numbers | $n$ |
| First n even numbers | $n+1$ |
| Squares of the first n naturals | $\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ |
| Cubes of the first n naturals | $\dfrac{n(n+1)^2}{4}$ |

> **Tip:** First 30 even numbers average $30 + 1 = 31$. First 25 odd numbers average 25. No adding needed.

### Numbers with equal gaps
Consecutive numbers, consecutive even or odd numbers, and multiples of k all climb by one fixed step. Their average is the **middle term**, which is also $\dfrac{\text{first} + \text{last}}{2}$.

> **Example:** 7 consecutive even numbers average 48. The middle (4th) number is 48. Step up by 2, three times: largest = $48 + 6 = 54$.

Multiples of 6 up to 100 run from 6 to 96. Average = $\dfrac{6 + 96}{2} = 51$.

### Close numbers: the assumed-mean method
To average numbers huddled close together, pick a round value nearby. Write each number's gap (+ or −) from it. Average the gaps. Add the result back.

284, 291, 296, 302, 307 sit around 300. Gaps: $-16, -9, -4, +2, +7$. Gap total = $-20$. Average gap = $-20 \div 5 = -4$. Average = $300 - 4 = 296$.

> **Tip:** This method replaces one big addition with small ones. Use it for lists of marks, weights or prices.

patterns.name: Sum from average / one missing value
patterns.howToSpot: An average and a count are given. The total is asked, or one value is missing from a list of known values.
steps: Multiply the average by the count to get the sum.
Add up the values you already know.
Subtract: what is left is the missing value (or the asked total).
patterns.why: The average is only the sum shared equally, so the sum carries all the information.

example.q: The average of 5 numbers is 27. Four of them are 20, 31, 25 and 18. Find the fifth number.

patterns.name: Average of standard series
patterns.howToSpot: 'Find the average of the first n natural / odd / even numbers', or of their squares or cubes.
steps: Spot the series and n, the count of terms.
Take the average straight from the table.
For even numbers ending at 2n, n is half the last term.
patterns.why: Each table value is the series-sum formula already divided by n.

example.q: Find the average of the first 30 even natural numbers.

patterns.name: Consecutive numbers and equal gaps
patterns.howToSpot: 'The average of 7 consecutive even numbers is 48 — find the largest', or the average of the multiples of k in a range.
steps: Place the average at the middle term of the list.
Step out from the middle by the gap (1 for consecutive, 2 for even/odd, k for multiples).
For a range of multiples, use (first + last) ÷ 2.
patterns.why: Equal gaps balance on both sides of the middle, so the middle term is the mean.

example.q: The average of 9 consecutive odd numbers is 45. Find the smallest of them.

patterns.name: Same operation on every value
patterns.howToSpot: 'Each number is multiplied by 4 / increased by 6 / divided by 2' — the new average is asked.
patterns.formula: \text{new average} = k \times A + c \quad (\text{same order as stated})
steps: Do to the old average exactly what is done to each value.
Keep the stated order of operations.
Addition shifts the average; multiplication scales it.
patterns.why: A uniform change moves the sum and the average exactly the way it moves each single value.

example.q: The average of 7 numbers is 18. Each number is increased by 4 and then divided by 2. Find the new average.

patterns.name: Assumed mean (deviation method)
patterns.howToSpot: A short list of 4-8 close numbers (weights, marks, runs) is given and their average is asked.
steps: Pick a round number near the middle.
Write each value's gap from it, with a + or − sign.
Add the gaps and divide by n.
Add the result to the assumed value.
patterns.why: Shifting every value by the same amount shifts the average by that amount.

example.q: Find the average of 396, 402, 407, 413 and 417.

revision: Sum = average × count. Work in sums, divide at the end.
Every value + k → average + k; every value × k → average × k.
Equal gaps → average = middle term = (first + last)/2.
First n naturals $\frac{n+1}{2}$; first n odd $n$; first n even $n+1$.
Squares $\frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$; cubes $\frac{n(n+1)^2}{4}$.
Close numbers → assumed mean + average of the gaps.

subtopics.title: Members joining or leaving
subtopics.concept:
When a member joins or leaves and the average changes, work with **totals**, not averages.

- Join: newcomer = new average + n × rise, with n the OLD count.
- Leave: leaver = old total − new total of the rest.
- Replace: new value = old value + n × (change in average). The count does not change.

A wrongly copied value shifts the total by (correct − wrong), so the average shifts by that ÷ n.

formulas.name: Joining member
formulas.note: n = old count; A' = new average.

formulas.name: Leaving member
formulas.note: A' = average of the remaining n members.

tricks.title: Joining: own share plus extras
tricks.body: New value = new average + (old count) × (average jump).

example.q: The average age of 30 students is 14 years. Their teacher joins them and the average becomes 15 years. Find the teacher's age.

tricks.title: Replacement: the jump times n
tricks.body: Only the swapped item changes the sum, and it changes by n × (average jump).

example.q: The average of 8 numbers is 24. If 20 is replaced by 44, find the new average.

tricks.title: Exclusion: subtract the totals
tricks.body: Old total − (new count × new average) = the removed value.

example.q: The average of 9 numbers is 27. One number is excluded and the average of the rest becomes 25. Find the excluded number.

mistakes.wrong: Using the old average where the new one belongs.
mistakes.right: Label both averages first: A old, B new. The formula reads off B for shares.

mistakes.wrong: Counting the newcomer inside n.
mistakes.right: In the joining formula, n is the count BEFORE the newcomer arrives.

mistakes.wrong: For a replacement, changing the new number by just the average jump.
mistakes.right: The swap changes the total by n × jump, so the new value moves by n × jump.

mistakes.wrong: Subtracting when the average rises (or adding when it falls).
mistakes.right: Fix the sign from the story: rise = plus, fall = minus, for joiners and replacements alike.

mistakes.wrong: Correcting a wrong entry by editing the average directly.
mistakes.right: Adjust the total by (correct − wrong), then divide by n.

subtopics.notes:
### The habit: work with totals
A group has an average. Then one member joins, leaves, or is swapped out, and the average changes. Averages cannot be added or removed. Totals can.

1. Old total = old count × old average.
2. New total = new count × new average.
3. The joining or leaving value is the difference of the two totals.

> **Rule:** Never move an average. Move the total (count × average), then divide at the end.

### Someone joins
n members average A. One person joins, and the n + 1 members average B.

$$\text{newcomer} = (n+1)B - nA = B + n(B - A)$$

In words: the newcomer carries his own share B, plus the rise $B - A$ for each of the n old members.

> **Example:** 24 students average 15 years. With the teacher included, the average becomes 16. Teacher = $16 + 24 \times 1 = 40$ years. Check: $25 \times 16 - 24 \times 15 = 40$.

### Someone leaves
n members average A. One leaves, and the remaining $n-1$ average B.

$$\text{leaver} = nA - (n-1)B$$

11 numbers average 36, so the sum is 396. One number is removed; the other 10 average 34, sum 340. Removed number = $396 - 340 = 56$.

> **Watch:** If the average falls after someone leaves, the leaver was above the old average. If it rises, the leaver was below it.

### Someone is replaced
The count stays n. Only the total changes, and it changes by $n \times$ (change in average).

$$\text{new value} = \text{old value} + n \times (\text{change in average})$$

The average weight of 8 people rises by 2.5 kg when one person is replaced. The old person weighed 65 kg. New person = $65 + 8 \times 2.5 = 85$ kg. If the average falls, subtract instead. If TWO members are replaced, their pair's total changes by $n \times$ change — split it between them as the question directs.

### A wrong entry is found
A value was copied wrongly — say 84 was read as 48. The total is off by exactly (correct − wrong).

$$\text{correct average} = \text{wrong average} + \frac{\text{correct} - \text{wrong}}{n}$$

30 students average 62 marks, with 84 read as 48. Correct average = $62 + \dfrac{36}{30} = 63.2$. With two errors, add both corrections, with their signs, before dividing.

### A whole group joins
k new members join n old ones, and the average becomes B.

$$\text{group total} = (n+k)B - nA, \qquad \text{group average} = \frac{(n+k)B - nA}{k}$$

30 students average 12 years. Ten new students join and the average becomes 13. Newcomers' total = $40 \times 13 - 30 \times 12 = 160$. Their average = $160 \div 10 = 16$ years. If k members LEAVE instead, their total = $nA - (n-k)B$ — the same bridge, walked the other way.

> **Tip:** Check every answer: new total ÷ new count must equal the stated new average.

patterns.name: One member joins — find the newcomer
patterns.howToSpot: A teacher, manager or new player joins a group and the average age, salary or weight moves by a given amount.
steps: Write the old total nA and the new total (n+1)B.
Subtract: the newcomer is the difference.
Shortcut: newcomer = B + n × rise. If the average falls, the rise is negative.
patterns.why: The newcomer supplies his own share and lifts every old member by the change.

example.q: The average age of 24 students is 15 years. Including their teacher, it becomes 16 years. Find the teacher's age.

patterns.name: One member leaves — the removed value
patterns.howToSpot: 'One number is excluded / one member leaves, and the average of the rest becomes …'.
steps: Subtract the two totals; divide later only if the new average is asked instead.
patterns.why: Removing one value changes the sum and the count by known amounts, and nothing else.

example.q: The average of 12 numbers is 40. One number is removed and the average of the remaining numbers is 38. Find the removed number.

patterns.name: One member is replaced
patterns.howToSpot: 'A new man replaces one weighing 65 kg and the average increases by 2.5 kg.' The count does not change.
steps: Keep the count n the same.
Change in total = n × change in average.
New member = old member + that change (subtract if the average fell).
patterns.why: Only one value changed, so the whole change in the total belongs to it.

example.q: The average weight of 9 persons falls by 2 kg when a person weighing 78 kg is replaced by a newcomer. Find the newcomer's weight.

patterns.name: A wrongly recorded value is corrected
patterns.howToSpot: 'Later it was found that 84 had been misread as 48.' The correct average is asked.
steps: For each error, work out (correct value − wrong value), keeping the sign.
Divide by n and add to the wrong average.
patterns.why: An error changes the total by exactly (correct − wrong) and nothing else.

example.q: The average of 25 marks was calculated as 48. Later, 72 was found to have been misread as 27. Find the correct average.

patterns.name: A whole group joins or leaves
patterns.howToSpot: k new students join (or k leave), the new overall average is given, and the group's own average is asked.
steps: Old total = nA; new total = (n + k)B.
The difference is the joining group's total.
Divide by k for their average. For a swap of k members, the total changes by n × change.
patterns.why: The same total bridge as for a single member, taken k people at once.

example.q: 30 students have an average age of 12 years. 10 new students join and the average becomes 13 years. Find the average age of the new students.

revision: Join: newcomer $= B + n(B - A)$, n = old count.
Leave: leaver $= nA - (n-1)B$.
Replace: new = old ± n × (change in average).
Wrong entry: average shifts by (correct − wrong) ÷ n.
Group joins: group total = (n+k)B − nA, then ÷ k for their average.
Check: new total ÷ new count = stated new average.

subtopics.title: Weighted average & two-group problems
subtopics.concept:
When groups of different sizes are combined, the combined average is the **weighted** mean:

total of all values ÷ total count. Turn each group's average into a total (size × average) first.

The combined average always sits closer to the bigger group's average. With equal group sizes it is the plain middle of the two averages.

With two group averages and the combined average known, the group sizes sit in the reverse ratio of their distances from the combined average.

formulas.name: Missing group average
formulas.note: N = total count, overall average known.

tricks.title: Totals, not averages
tricks.body: Turn each group into a total, add, divide by the combined count.

example.q: In a class of 60 students, the 20 girls average 40 marks. The class average is 50. Find the boys' average.

tricks.title: Feel the balance point
tricks.body: The combined average splits the gap between the group averages in the ratio n₂ : n₁, the reverse of the sizes.

example.q: 20 boys average 12 years and 30 girls average 11 years. Find the combined average age.
steps: The answer sits 0.4 above 11 and 0.6 below 12 — closer to the girls, the bigger group.

tricks.title: One newcomer is a tiny second group
tricks.body: A single new member changing a group average is just a weighted average with k = 1. Use value = B + n(B − A).

example.q: 15 workers average ₹250 in daily wages. A manager joins and the average becomes ₹300. Find the manager's wage.

mistakes.wrong: Averaging the two averages when the groups differ in size.
mistakes.right: Weight each average by its group size: (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂).

mistakes.wrong: Dividing by the wrong count (students + teacher, workers + manager).
mistakes.right: List every member of the combined group before dividing.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the balance ratio forwards (closer group = smaller).
mistakes.right: The group closer to the combined average is the bigger one.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding a total halfway through.
mistakes.right: These questions come out exact. A messy decimal mid-way means a slip, so recheck the totals.

mistakes.wrong: Group averages that do not bracket the combined average.
mistakes.right: The combined average must sit between the group averages. If not, re-read the question.

subtopics.notes:
### Why averaging averages fails
Section A has 20 students with average 60. Section B has 80 students with average 40. The middle of 60 and 40 is 50, but the real class average is $\dfrac{20 \times 60 + 80 \times 40}{100} = 44$.

The bigger section pulls the answer towards its own average. So each group must be weighted by its size.

> **Rule:** Combined average = (sum of all group totals) ÷ (sum of all sizes). A group total = size × its average.

### The weighted-average method
Work in three moves, every time.

1. Total of each group = size × average.
2. Add all the totals. Add all the sizes.
3. Divide.

> **Example:** 30 boys average 42 kg and 20 girls average 37 kg. Combined = $\dfrac{1260 + 740}{50} = 40$ kg.

### Where the combined average sits
Three facts that kill wrong options without calculation:

- It always lies between the smallest and the largest group average.
- It lies closer to the average of the **bigger** group.
- Equal group sizes → it is the plain middle of the group averages.

> **Tip:** If an option sits outside the two group averages, cross it out at once.

### One group's average missing
Class of 40 averages 65 marks. The 25 boys average 62. Find the girls' average.

Class total = $40 \times 65 = 2600$. Boys' total = $25 \times 62 = 1550$. Girls' total = $2600 - 1550 = 1050$ over 15 girls → 70.

> **Rule:** Missing total = overall total − known totals. Then divide by that group's own size.

### Finding the sizes: the balance method
Both group averages and the combined average are known; a size is asked. The sizes sit in the **reverse** ratio of the distances from the combined average:

$$\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{\bar{x}_2 - \bar{x}}{\bar{x} - \bar{x}_1}$$

Class average 58, boys 62, girls 52. Distances: boys 4, girls 6. So boys : girls = $6 : 4 = 3 : 2$.

Picture a see-saw: the heavier group sits closer to the balance point. Scale the ratio up to the given total when a count is asked.

> **Watch:** The group closer to the combined average is the bigger one. Reversing this ratio is the classic wrong option.

### Sizes given as a ratio or a fraction
No real counts? Use the ratio parts as the counts.

Boys : girls = 3 : 2, averages 150 cm and 140 cm → $\dfrac{3 \times 150 + 2 \times 140}{5} = 146$ cm.

"One-fourth of a class averages 72 and the whole class averages 60." Take the class as 4 parts: $4 \times 60 = 240 = 72 + 3x$, so the other three parts average $x = 56$.

> **Tip:** The weighted average depends only on the proportions, never on the actual headcount.

patterns.name: Combined average of two or more groups
patterns.howToSpot: Two or three groups (boys/girls, sections, batches) with sizes and averages; the overall average is asked.
steps: Multiply each group's size by its average to get its total.
Add all the totals; add all the sizes.
Divide. The answer must lie closer to the bigger group's average.
patterns.why: An average is a total shared by a count, so only totals can be added.

example.q: In a school, 30 boys average 42 kg and 20 girls average 37 kg. Find the average weight of all 50 students.

patterns.name: Missing average of one group
patterns.howToSpot: The overall average and one group's average are given; the other group's average is asked.
steps: Overall total = total count × overall average.
Divide the rest by the other group's size.
patterns.why: The two group totals must add up to the overall total.

example.q: The average marks of 40 students is 65. The 25 boys average 62 marks. Find the girls' average.

patterns.name: Group ratio from the averages
patterns.howToSpot: All three averages are known (two groups plus combined) and the ratio of sizes is asked.
steps: Find how far each group average is from the combined average.
The sizes are in the reverse ratio of these distances.
Scale the ratio to the given total if a count is asked.
patterns.why: The surplus above the mean from one group must balance the shortfall from the other.

example.q: A class averages 58 marks. The boys average 62 and the girls 52. Find boys : girls.
steps: Sizes are the reverse: boys : girls = $6 : 4 = 3 : 2$.

patterns.name: Sizes given as a ratio or fraction
patterns.howToSpot: 'Boys and girls are in the ratio 3 : 2' or 'one-fourth of the students average …' instead of real counts.
steps: Use the ratio parts (or fraction parts) as if they were the counts.
For a missing average, solve the one equation that is left.
patterns.why: The weighted average depends only on the proportions of the groups.

example.q: Boys and girls in a class are in the ratio 3 : 2. Boys average 150 cm in height and girls 140 cm. Find the average height of the class.
steps: Take 3 parts of boys and 2 of girls.

patterns.name: A group count from the averages
patterns.howToSpot: The overall average and both group averages are known, one group's count is known, and the other count (or total) is asked.
steps: Find the two distances from the overall average.
The sizes follow the reverse ratio; pair each size with the group on the far side.
Scale the ratio by the known group's count, then add for the total.
patterns.why: Once the size ratio is fixed, the known count prices one part of it.

example.q: A firm pays an average salary of ₹8,000. Its 7 technicians earn ₹12,000 each and the rest earn ₹6,000 each. How many employees does the firm have in total?

revision: Combined average = sum of (size × average) ÷ sum of sizes.
Missing group: overall total − known totals, then ÷ its own size.
Sizes = reverse ratio of distances from the combined average.
Ratio or fraction given → use the parts as counts.
Combined average sits closer to the bigger group.

subtopics.title: Batsman problems, overlapping sums & multi-step sets
subtopics.concept:
**Batsman template:** a score of x in the nth innings lifts the average by d. The new average is $x - (n-1)d$; the score itself was (new total) − (old total).

**Overlapping windows:** averages over two overlapping stretches differ only at their ends. Thu − Mon = 3 × (difference of the averages) for three-day windows.

**Split sets and ages:** turn every average into a sum, use one variable for the unknown part, and remember a fixed group's average age rises by 1 each year.

formulas.name: Overlap subtraction
formulas.note: Three-day windows; multiply by the overlap length.

tricks.title: Batsman: stay in totals
tricks.body: Old total + new score = new count × new average.

example.q: A batsman scores 87 in his 17th innings and raises his average by 3. Find his average after the 17th innings.

tricks.title: Overlaps: subtract the sums
tricks.body: Shared days cancel, leaving only the difference of the end days.

example.q: The average temperature of Mon, Tue and Wed is 37°C; of Tue, Wed and Thu it is 34°C. If Monday was 40°C, find Thursday.

tricks.title: One variable for the unknown chunk
tricks.body: Name the smallest unknown x, express the rest through it, and close the equation with the leftover sum.

example.q: 8 numbers average 20. The first two average 15.5 and the next three average $\dfrac{64}{3}$. The 6th number is 5 less than the 7th, and the 8th is 7 more than the 7th. Find the 8th number.

mistakes.wrong: In batsman questions, multiplying by n for the old total.
mistakes.right: Before the nth innings there are only n − 1 innings. Old total = (n − 1) × old average.

mistakes.wrong: Reporting the difference of two overlapping averages as the end-day difference.
mistakes.right: Multiply the difference of averages by the overlap length (3 days → × 3).

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the two halves of 11 numbers share the 6th number.
mistakes.right: First 6 + last 6 = 12 counts for 11 numbers: the middle one is counted twice.

mistakes.wrong: Setting a relation backwards ('the 6th is 5 less than the 7th').
mistakes.right: Translate carefully: 6th = 7th − 5, so 7th = 6th + 5.

mistakes.wrong: Treating a bowling average like a batsman average (higher = better).
mistakes.right: A bowler improves when the average falls. Use $aW + r = (a-d)(W+w)$.

subtopics.notes:
### Batsman: the innings question
A batsman's average = total runs ÷ innings played. The standard question: he scores x runs in his nth innings and the average rises by d. Let the new average be A. Then:

$$(n-1)(A - d) + x = nA \quad\Rightarrow\quad A = x - (n-1)d$$

98 runs in the 20th innings lift the average by 2 → new average = $98 - 19 \times 2 = 60$.

> **Rule:** Score in the nth innings = new average + (n − 1) × rise. It must feed every past innings plus its own share.

The reverse question asks how many runs are needed. To lift an average from 42 to 45 in the 11th innings: needed = $11 \times 45 - 10 \times 42 = 75$.

### Bowler's average
A bowler's average = runs given ÷ wickets taken, and a LOWER value is better. Average a, then a match of w wickets for r runs makes it fall by d. With W wickets before the match:

$$aW + r = (a - d)(W + w)$$

Average 12.4; a match of 5 wickets for 26 runs improves it by 0.4 → $12.4W + 26 = 12(W + 5)$, so $W = 85$.

> **Watch:** "Improves" means the bowling average falls. Subtract, never add.

### Overlapping windows
The average of Mon–Wed is 37 and of Tue–Thu is 34. The two sums share Tue and Wed, so subtracting kills them:

$$\text{Thu} - \text{Mon} = 3 \times (34 - 37) = -9$$

Mon was 40°, so Thu = $40 - 9 = 31$°. Multiply the difference of averages by the length of the overlap.

### First-k and last-k share a middle
13 numbers average 30. The first 7 average 27 and the last 7 average 35. The 7th number sits in both halves, so it is counted twice:

$$\text{middle} = 7 \times 27 + 7 \times 35 - 13 \times 30 = 189 + 245 - 390 = 44$$

> **Tip:** Add the two part-sums and subtract the whole. What survives is the shared item.

### Split sets with relations
"The average of 6 numbers is 30. The first two average 24, the next two 33. Of the last two, one is 4 more than the other."

Sums first: total 180, first pair 48, second pair 66, so the last pair totals 66. Name the smaller x: $x + (x + 4) = 66$, so 31 and 35.

> **Rule:** Every average becomes a sum. Name ONE unknown x and write the rest in terms of it.

### Ages move together
Every member of a fixed group gets one year older each year, so the average age also rises by 1 per year.

- n years ago the group's average was A → today it is $A + n$ (same members).
- At the birth of the youngest: subtract the youngest's age from every member, and drop the youngest from the count. Five members average 24, youngest 8 → $\dfrac{120 - 5 \times 8}{4} = 20$.

> **Tip:** Rebuild the story with totals — old total, change, new total, new count. If new total ÷ new count misses the stated average, a step is wrong.

patterns.name: Batsman: the innings that moves the average
patterns.howToSpot: 'Scores x in his nth innings and raises his average by d', or 'how many runs in the next innings to reach a target average'.
steps: Write old total = (n − 1)(A − d) and new total = nA for the new average A.
Solve for A, or subtract old total from target total when runs needed are asked.
patterns.why: The new score must lift every earlier innings by d and still leave its own share A.

example.q: A batsman scores 98 runs in his 20th innings and raises his average by 2. Find his new average.

patterns.name: Overlapping windows
patterns.howToSpot: Averages over two overlapping stretches — Mon–Wed and Tue–Thu, or the first 7 and last 7 of 13 numbers.
steps: Subtract the sums: the shared items cancel, leaving the end difference. For first-k/last-k, ADD and subtract the whole: the shared middle survives.
Use the extra fact (one end value, or a ratio) to finish.
patterns.why: Shared values appear in both sums, so they vanish on subtraction and double up on addition.

example.q: The average of 13 numbers is 30. The average of the first 7 is 27 and of the last 7 is 35. Find the 7th number.

patterns.name: Split set with relations between unknowns
patterns.howToSpot: Averages of parts of a list, plus a tie such as 'one number is 4 more than the other'.
steps: Change every average into a sum.
Find the leftover sum for the unknown values.
Write the unknowns with one variable x from the relation, then solve.
patterns.why: Once everything is a sum, the question is one equation in one variable.

example.q: Six numbers average 30. The first two average 24 and the next two 33. Of the last two, one is 4 more than the other. Find the larger of the last two.

patterns.name: Ages over time
patterns.howToSpot: Average ages 'n years ago' or 'at the birth of the youngest', with members added later.
patterns.formula: \text{average after } t \text{ years} = A + t \quad (\text{same members})
steps: Bring every average to the SAME year: add t for each year passed.
Work in totals; include or remove members as the story demands.
At a member's birth: subtract that age from every member, and drop one from the count.
patterns.why: Each person ages one year per year, so a fixed group's total rises by n per year.

example.q: A family of 5 members has an average age of 24 years. The youngest is 8. What was the average age of the family at the birth of the youngest?
steps: 8 years ago everyone was 8 younger: $120 - 5 \times 8 = 80$ years over 4 members.

patterns.name: Bowling average
patterns.howToSpot: 'A bowler's average is 12.4 runs per wicket; he takes 5 wickets for 26 runs and the average improves by 0.4.'
steps: Let W be the wickets before the match; runs given so far = aW.
After the match: runs aW + r, wickets W + w, average a − d.
Solve the linear equation for W.
patterns.why: A bowling average is a runs-per-wicket average, so the same total bridge applies.

example.q: A bowler's average is 12.4 runs per wicket. In a match he takes 5 wickets for 26 runs, and his average improves by 0.4. How many wickets did he have before this match?

revision: Batsman: new average = x − (n − 1)d; needed runs = new total − old total.
Bowler: aW + r = (a − d)(W + w); 'improves' means falls.
Overlap: end difference = overlap length × difference of averages.
First-k and last-k: shared middle = part sums − whole sum.
Split set: sums first, then one variable x.
Fixed group: average age +1 per year; at a birth, subtract that age from everyone.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The average age of 30 students is 14. With the teacher, the average goes up by 1."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Turn each average into a total (average × number of people).
The newcomer is the difference of the two totals.

example.q: The average age of 30 students is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average rises by 1 year. Find the teacher's age.
example.solution:
Students' total = 30 × 14 = 420
With teacher: 31 people × 15 = 465
Teacher = 465 − 420 = **45 years**

pyqPatterns.pattern: One member is replaced (or one wrong entry)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One person is replaced, or one value was copied wrongly, and the average changes by a known amount.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Total change = number of people × change in average.
Add it to the old person's value (subtract if the average fell).

example.q: The average weight of 10 men rises by 1.5 kg when one man weighing 58 kg is replaced by a new man. Find the new man's weight.
example.solution:
Total rise = 10 × 1.5 = 15 kg
New man = old man + rise
58 + 15 = **73 kg**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Batsman's average after one more innings
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Scores 87 in his 17th innings and his average rises by 3."
pyqPatterns.approach:
The new score first lifts the 16 earlier innings by 3 each.
What is left of the score is the new average.

example.q: A batsman scores 87 runs in his 17th innings and his average rises by 3. Find his new average.
example.solution:
Lifting 16 earlier innings by 3 = 16 × 3 = 48 runs
New average = 87 − 48 = 39
Check: old average 36, so 16 × 36 + 87 = 663 = 17 × 39
New average = **39**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "30 boys average 42 kg and 20 girls average 37 kg. Find the class average."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find each group's total (number × average).
Add the totals and divide by all the people.

example.q: 30 boys average 42 kg and 20 girls average 37 kg. Find the class average.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Both group averages and the overall average are given; asks the ratio of the two groups.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find how far each group's average is from the overall average.
The ratio is those two distances swapped.

example.q: The class average is 58; boys average 62 and girls 52. Find boys : girls.
example.solution:
Boys are 62 − 58 = 4 away
Girls are 58 − 52 = 6 away
Swap them: boys : girls = 6 : 4
= **3 : 2**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Average of a run of numbers
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Average of all multiples of 6 between 1 and 100" or "average of the first n odd numbers".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Evenly spaced numbers: average = (first + last) ÷ 2.
First n counting numbers (1, 2, 3, …): average = (n + 1) ÷ 2.

example.q: Find the average of all multiples of 6 between 1 and 100.
example.solution:
Multiples: 6, 12, 18, …, 96 (next is 102, too big)
First + last = 6 + 96 = 102
102 ÷ 2 = **51**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Average and count given with some numbers known, or every number is multiplied or increased by the same amount.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Total = average × count. Subtract the known numbers to find a missing one.
A change done to every number is done to the average too, in the same order.

example.q: The average of 6 numbers is 15. Each number is multiplied by 3 and then increased by 5. Find the new average.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two parts of one list overlap, e.g. the first 6 and the last 6 of 11 numbers.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Turn every average into a total.
Add the two part totals, then subtract the whole total. What is left is the shared number.

example.q: The average of 11 numbers is 50. The first 6 average 49 and the last 6 average 52. Find the 6th number.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Ages in the past or future
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Five years ago the average age was …" and then a child or new member is added.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Move every age to the same year (each person adds 1 year per year).
Then use totals and adjust the head count.

example.q: Five years ago the average age of a husband and wife was 25. Now the average of husband, wife and child is 22. Find the child's age.
example.solution:
Couple 5 years ago: 2 × 25 = 50
Couple now: 50 + 5 + 5 = 60
Family now: 3 × 22 = 66
Child = 66 − 60 = **6 years**

solvedExamples.q: The average of 8 numbers is 32.5. What is the sum of these numbers?
The average age of 20 boys is 12 years and that of 30 girls is 11 years. The average age of all the students is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: Weighted mean: the bigger group (girls) pulls the answer to 11.4 — closer to 11 than to 12.

solvedExamples.q: The average of 9 numbers is 27. If one number is excluded, the average of the remaining numbers becomes 25. The excluded number is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: Total sums both ways and subtract — no formula needed.

solvedExamples.q: The average of 8 numbers is 24. If the number 20 is replaced by 44, the new average will be:
solvedExamples.solution:
Increase in sum $= 44 - 20 = 24$.
Increase in average $= \frac{24}{8} = 3$ ⇒ new average $= 27$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Average jumps by (change in the number)/8 = 24/8 = 3 ⇒ 24 + 3 = 27.

solvedExamples.q: A batsman scores 87 runs in his 17th innings and thus increases his average by 3 runs. His average after the 17th innings is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the average after 17 innings be A.
Before: 16 innings at $(A - 3)$.
$16(A - 3) + 87 = 17A$ ⇒ $16A - 48 + 87 = 17A$ ⇒ $A = 39$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: New total = old total + 87: 17A = 16(A−3) + 87 ⇒ A = 39. (Quick check: old avg 36, total 576; 576 + 87 = 663 = 17 × 39 ✓)

practice.q: The average of the first 10 natural numbers is:
practice.shortcut: Consecutive 1–10: average = middle pair (5 + 6)/2 = 5.5.

practice.q: The average of 5 numbers is 27. If one more number 37 is included, the new average is:
practice.solution:
Old sum $= 135$. New sum $= 135 + 37 = 172$.
New average $= \frac{172}{6} = 28.5$.
practice.shortcut: 37 is 10 above the old average; the extra 10 spreads over 6 numbers: 27 + 10/6 = 28.5.

practice.q: The average of 6 numbers is 15. If each number is multiplied by 3 and then increased by 5, the new average is:
practice.shortcut: Linear operations pass through the average: ×3 then +5 ⇒ 50.

practice.q: The average of 5 consecutive numbers is 30. The largest of these numbers is:
practice.solution:
The middle (3rd) number is the average = 30.
Numbers: 28, 29, 30, 31, 32 ⇒ largest **32**.
practice.shortcut: Average = middle term ⇒ largest = 30 + 2 = 32.

practice.q: A batsman made 38.5 runs on average in 10 innings. His total runs are:
practice.shortcut: Sum = average × innings = 385.

practice.q: The average age of 30 students in a class is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average age increases by one year. The teacher's age is:
practice.shortcut: Newcomer = new average + n × (jump) = 15 + 30 × 1 = 45.

practice.q: The average of 11 numbers is 50. The average of the first 6 numbers is 49 and that of the last 6 is 52. The 6th number is:
practice.shortcut: The 6th number is counted in both chunks: chunk sums add to total + 6th ⇒ 6th = 606 − 550 = 56.

practice.q: A batsman scores 87 runs in his 17th innings, which increases his average by 3 runs. His average after the 17th innings is:
The average marks of 60 students in a class is 50. The average marks of the 20 girls is 40. The average marks of the boys is:
practice.shortcut: Alligation too: 20 : 40 (girls : boys) splits the 40–55... the combined 50 sits 10 from girls' 40 and 5 from boys' 55 ⇒ sizes 2 : 1 ✓.

practice.q: The average monthly wage of 15 workers is ₹250. A manager is appointed and the average wage becomes ₹300. The manager's monthly wage is:
practice.shortcut: Manager = 300 + 15 × 50 = ₹1,050 (his own share plus the ₹50 raise for each of the 15).

practice.q: The average of the squares of the first 10 natural numbers is:
The average temperature of Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday is 37°C and of Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday is 34°C. If the temperature on Monday was 40°C, the temperature on Thursday is:
practice.shortcut: Thursday = Monday − 3 × (37 − 34) = 40 − 9 = 31.

practice.q: The average weight of three men A, B and C is 84 kg. A fourth man D joins them and the average weight of the four becomes 80 kg. If A weighs 78 kg and E replaces A, the average weight of B, C, D and E becomes 79 kg. E's weight is:
practice.shortcut: Build every sum stepwise: 252 → D = 68 → B + C = 174 → E = 316 − 242 = 74.

practice.q: The average of 8 numbers is 20. The average of the first two is 15.5 and that of the next three is $21\frac{1}{3}$. If the 6th number is 5 less than the 7th and the 8th is 7 more than the 7th, the 8th number is:
practice.solution:
Total = 160. First five total = 31 + 64 = 95.
Last three total = 65. Let the 6th be x: 6th + 7th + 8th = x + (x + 5) + (x + 12).
$3x + 17 = 65$ ⇒ $x = 16$ ⇒ 8th $= 16 + 12 = 28$.
practice.shortcut: Leftover sum 65 across three numbers whose mean is 65/3 — anchor on the 7th: 6th = 7th − 5, 8th = 7th + 7 ⇒ 7th = 21 ⇒ 8th = 28.

practice.q: The average age of a husband and wife at the time of their marriage was 23 years. After 5 years they have a one-year-old child. The average age of the family of three now is:
practice.solution:
Marriage total = 2 × 23 = 46. After 5 years: 46 + 5 + 5 = 56.
Child adds 1 year: total = 57.
Average $= \frac{57}{3} = 19$ years.
practice.shortcut: Both adults age 5 (total 56), child is 1 ⇒ 57/3 = 19. (Trap: forgetting to add the child's own age.)

practice.q: The average of 12 numbers is 45.5. The sum of these numbers is:
The average of five numbers is 36. Four of the numbers are 30, 42, 28 and 45. The fifth number is:
practice.shortcut: Gaps from 36: −6, +6, −8, +9 → total +1, so the fifth must be 1 below 36 = 35.

practice.q: The average of the first 25 odd natural numbers is:
practice.solution: Average of the first n odd numbers is n → $25$. Check: sum $= 25^2 = 625$, $625 \div 25 = 25$.

practice.q: The average of the first 20 even natural numbers is:
practice.solution: Average of the first n even numbers is $n + 1 = 21$. (2 to 40 → $\frac{2+40}{2} = 21$.)

practice.q: The average of the cubes of the first 8 natural numbers is:
practice.shortcut: Direct: $\frac{n(n+1)^2}{4} = \frac{8 \times 81}{4} = 162$.

practice.q: The average of 7 consecutive even numbers is 48. The largest of them is:
practice.shortcut: Largest = middle + 3 × 2 = 54. (51 comes from stepping by 1.)

practice.q: The average of all the multiples of 6 between 1 and 100 is:
practice.shortcut: Equal gaps → (first + last)/2 — no need to count the terms.

practice.q: The average of five consecutive natural numbers is n. If the next two consecutive numbers are also included, the average of the seven numbers becomes:
practice.solution:
Numbers: $n-2, n-1, n, n+1, n+2$ (sum $5n$). Next two: $n+3, n+4$.
New sum $= 5n + 2n + 7 = 7n + 7$ → average $= n + 1$.
practice.shortcut: Seven consecutive numbers from n−2 to n+4 → middle term is n+1.

practice.q: The average of 8 numbers is 21. If each number is multiplied by 4, the new average is:
practice.solution: Multiplying every value by 4 multiplies the average by 4: $21 \times 4 = 84$.

practice.q: The average of 10 numbers is 40. Each number is first decreased by 6 and then divided by 2. The new average is:
practice.solution: Apply the same steps to the average: $(40 - 6) \div 2 = 17$.
practice.shortcut: Order matters: 40 ÷ 2 − 6 = 14 is the trap.

practice.q: Find the average of 284, 291, 296, 302 and 307.
The weights of six children are 48.5 kg, 52 kg, 50.5 kg, 47 kg, 54.5 kg and 53.5 kg. Their average weight is:
The average age of 24 students in a class is 15 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average becomes 16 years. The teacher's age is:
practice.solution: New total $= 25 \times 16 = 400$; old total $= 24 \times 15 = 360$. Teacher $= 40$ years.
practice.shortcut: Teacher $= 16 + 24 \times 1 = 40$.

practice.q: The average monthly salary of 20 employees is ₹18,000. When the manager's salary is added, the average rises by ₹1,500. The manager's monthly salary is:
practice.shortcut: $19500 + 20 \times 1500 = ₹49{,}500$. (₹48,000 uses the OLD average as his own share.)

practice.q: The average of 11 numbers is 36. If one number is removed, the average of the remaining numbers becomes 34. The number removed is:
practice.shortcut: Leaver $=$ new average $+ n \times$ fall $= 34 + 11 \times 2 = 56$.

practice.q: The average age of a family of 6 members is 28 years. If the age of the youngest member, 4 years, is excluded, the average age of the remaining members is:
practice.solution: Total $= 6 \times 28 = 168$. Without the youngest: $168 - 4 = 164$ for 5 members → $\frac{164}{5} = 32.8$ years.

practice.q: The average weight of 8 persons increases by 2.5 kg when a new person comes in place of one of them weighing 65 kg. The weight of the new person is:
practice.solution: Increase in total $= 8 \times 2.5 = 20$ kg. New person $= 65 + 20 = 85$ kg.

practice.q: When a teacher aged 48 years is replaced by a new teacher, the average age of the 12 teachers of a school decreases by 1.5 years. The age of the new teacher is:
practice.solution: Fall in total $= 12 \times 1.5 = 18$ years. New teacher $= 48 - 18 = 30$ years.
practice.shortcut: Average fell → the new person is younger by n × fall.

practice.q: The average of 5 numbers increases by 3 when two of them, 12 and 18, are replaced by two new numbers. The average of the two new numbers is:
practice.solution:
Increase in total $= 5 \times 3 = 15$.
New pair's sum $= 12 + 18 + 15 = 45$ → average $= 22.5$.
practice.shortcut: 18 comes from adding 3 to the old pair's average — the rise belongs to all 5 numbers.

practice.q: The average marks of 30 students were found to be 62. Later it was discovered that a score of 84 had been wrongly entered as 48. The correct average is:
The average of 50 observations was 36. It was later found that the observation 48 was wrongly taken as 23 and the observation 36 was wrongly taken as 60. The correct average is:
practice.solution:
Corrections: $48 - 23 = +25$ and $36 - 60 = -24$ → net $+1$.
Correct total $= 1800 + 1 = 1801$ → average $= 36.02$.
practice.shortcut: Adding both differences as +25 and +24 gives the trap 36.98.

practice.q: The average age of 30 students is 12 years. When 10 new students join, the average age becomes 13 years. The average age of the new students is:
practice.solution: New total $= 40 \times 13 = 520$; old $= 360$. New students' total $= 160$ → average 16 years.
practice.shortcut: Each newcomer: $13 + \frac{30 \times 1}{10} = 16$.

practice.q: The average weight of 45 students is 52 kg. Five students whose average weight is 48 kg leave, and five new students join in their place. The average weight of the class becomes 52.4 kg. The average weight of the five new students is:
practice.solution:
The count stays 45, so the total rises by $45 \times 0.4 = 18$ kg.
Leavers' total $= 5 \times 48 = 240$ → joiners' total $= 240 + 18 = 258$ → average $= 51.6$ kg.

practice.q: The average weight of 30 boys is 42 kg and that of 20 girls is 37 kg. The average weight of all 50 students is:
practice.shortcut: 39.5 is the simple average of 42 and 37 — wrong because the groups differ in size.

practice.q: Three sections of a class have 20, 30 and 50 students, whose average marks are 60, 70 and 54 respectively. The average marks of all the students are:
practice.shortcut: $61\frac{1}{3}$ is the unweighted mean of 60, 70, 54 — the trap.

practice.q: The average of 20 numbers is 15 and the average of another 30 numbers is 20. The average of all 50 numbers is:
The average marks of 40 students in a class is 65. If the average marks of the 25 boys is 62, the average marks of the girls is:
The average of 50 numbers is 38. If the average of the first 30 numbers is 36, the average of the remaining 20 numbers is:
practice.shortcut: First 30 are 2 below → 60 short; the 20 must cover it → $38 + \frac{60}{20} = 41$.

practice.q: The average marks of a class are 58. The boys average 62 and the girls average 52. The ratio of the number of boys to the number of girls is:
practice.shortcut: The group closer to the mean (boys, 4 away) is the larger group — 2 : 3 is the reversed-ratio trap.

practice.q: The average salary of all the workers in a workshop is ₹8,000. The average salary of 7 technicians is ₹12,000 and that of the rest is ₹6,000. The total number of workers is:
practice.shortcut: Technicians are 4000 above, the rest 2000 below → technicians : rest $= 1 : 2$ → rest $= 14$, total $= 21$.

practice.q: In a class of 48 students the average score is 71. The boys average 74 and the girls average 66. The number of girls is:
practice.shortcut: 30 is the number of boys — read what is asked.

practice.q: In a class, the ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 2. The average height of the boys is 150 cm and that of the girls is 140 cm. The average height of the class is:
practice.shortcut: 144 cm is the reversed-weights trap; 145 cm ignores the weights.

practice.q: The average marks of a class are 60. One-fourth of the students have an average of 72. The average marks of the remaining students are:
practice.solution: Take the class as 4 students: total $= 240$. One of them has 72, so the other 3 have $168$ → average $56$.
practice.shortcut: The quarter is 12 above; the other three-quarters must be $\frac{12}{3} = 4$ below → $56$.

practice.q: In a school, the ratio of boys to girls is 5 : 3. The average score of the whole school is 68 and the average score of the girls is 72. The average score of the boys is:
practice.solution: Take 5 boys and 3 girls: total $= 8 \times 68 = 544$; girls $= 216$; boys $= 328$ → $\frac{328}{5} = 65.6$.
practice.shortcut: Girls are 4 above: 3 × 4 = 12 extra, spread over 5 boys → boys are 2.4 below → $65.6$.

practice.q: A batsman scores 98 runs in his 20th innings and thereby increases his average by 2 runs. His average after the 20th innings is:
practice.solution: Let the new average be A. Then $19(A - 2) + 98 = 20A$ → $A = 98 - 38 = 60$.
practice.shortcut: $x - (n-1)d = 98 - 19 \times 2 = 60$. (58 is the OLD average.)

practice.q: A batsman has an average of 42 runs after 10 innings. How many runs must he score in the 11th innings to raise his average to 45?
practice.shortcut: $45 + 10 \times 3 = 75$ (own share + 3 for each earlier innings).

practice.q: A bowler's average is 12.4 runs per wicket. He takes 5 wickets for 26 runs in a match and his average improves by 0.4. The number of wickets he had taken before this match is:
practice.shortcut: 90 is the total AFTER the match.

practice.q: A bowler conceded runs at an average of 16 runs per wicket. In his next match he took 6 wickets for 30 runs, which lowered his average by 0.5. How many wickets had he taken before this match?
practice.shortcut: 132 is the count after the match; 63 forgets to divide by 0.5.

practice.q: The average of 13 numbers is 30. The average of the first 7 numbers is 27 and that of the last 7 numbers is 35. The 7th number is:
practice.solution: The 7th number is in both parts: $189 + 245 - 390 = 44$.

practice.q: The average temperature from Monday to Thursday was 37°C and from Tuesday to Friday was 38°C. If the temperatures on Monday and Friday were in the ratio 8 : 9, the temperature on Friday was:
practice.solution:
(Tue + Wed + Thu + Fri) − (Mon + Tue + Wed + Thu) $= 4 \times 38 - 4 \times 37 = 4$ → Fri − Mon $= 4$.
Ratio 8 : 9 differs by 1 part → 1 part $= 4$ → Friday $= 36$°C (Monday 32°C).

practice.q: The average of 6 numbers is 30. The average of the first two is 24 and that of the next two is 33. Of the remaining two numbers, one is 4 more than the other. The larger of these two numbers is:
practice.shortcut: Their average is 33, and they differ by 4 → 33 ± 2.

practice.q: The average of three numbers is 30. The first number is twice the second, and the second is three times the third. The largest number is:
practice.solution:
Let the third be x → second $3x$, first $6x$. Sum $10x = 90$ → $x = 9$.
Largest (first) $= 54$.

practice.q: The average age of a family of 5 members is 24 years. The youngest member is 8 years old. The average age of the family at the time of the birth of the youngest member was:
practice.solution:
Present total $= 120$. 8 years ago each of the 5 was 8 years younger: $120 - 40 = 80$.
But the youngest was just born (age 0), so only 4 members counted → $\frac{80}{4} = 20$ years.
practice.shortcut: 16 divides by 5 — the youngest did not yet exist.

practice.q: Five years ago, the average age of a husband and wife was 25 years. Today, the average age of the husband, the wife and their child is 22 years. The age of the child is:
practice.solution: Couple's total now $= 2 \times 25 + 10 = 60$. Family total $= 3 \times 22 = 66$. Child $= 6$ years.
practice.shortcut: 16 forgets that the couple aged 5 years each.

practice.q: The present average age of A, B and C is 30 years. Four years ago, the average age of B and C was 24 years. What will be A's age 4 years from now?
practice.solution: A + B + C $= 90$ now. B + C now $= 48 + 8 = 56$. So A $= 34$ now → 4 years hence $= 38$.
practice.shortcut: 46 forgets to age B and C by 4 years each.
